{"id": "80:26/q10", "question": "How does the split earth serve the passage's wider argument?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize either the provision that calls for gratitude or its role as evidence for resurrection and accountability; these functions can coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "80:26/q10/p1", "position": "The ordered provision of food displays God's power and mercy and calls for faith, gratitude, worship, and obedience.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the open reading anā introduces a necessarily incomplete account of God's provisioning because ordinary explanation cannot encompass its cosmic relations. Islahi says rain and opened earth pores are conditions no one else can provide. Kuranyolu says verses 18–20 discussed favors in human existence and nature, while this passage turns to external blessings sustaining life; its reminders strengthen faith and move people to grateful worship and obedience. Study Quran cites related descriptions of vegetation and water-revived earth at 6:99, 29:63, 30:24, 31:10, 35:27, and 39:21."}, {"id": "80:26/q10/p2", "position": "The food cycle, alongside human creation, demonstrates the possibility of resurrection and points toward accountability.", "reasons": "Biqai relates the call to warn those who fear at 79:45 to resurrection and receptive hearts: human creation and food make rejection astonishing. Islahi says the food argument parallels the creation argument, both showing resurrection possible through providential signs and ending in reward or punishment; he cites 21:30."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q01", "question": "How does growing grain follow the splitting of the earth?", "turns_on": "What the preceding earth-splitting denotes and how its order after rain and before grain works.", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q01/p1", "position": "The earth splits as plants grow through it, and the fāʾ marks grain as the ensuing stage of growth.", "reasons": "Bursevi says fīhā is the earth split by plants and the fāʾ marks succession. Al-Ālūsī says splitting widens progressively until grain forms; human plowing would interrupt the account of divine gifts. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows the interval required by the actual process. Ṭabāṭabāʾī traces rain, plant growth, and grain through 'then' and 'so'. Al-Ālūsī adds that the paired verbs and verbal nouns emphasize extraordinary divine provision."}, {"id": "80:27/q01/p2", "position": "The earlier splitting may be plowing or digging before the grain grows.", "reasons": "A view reported by al-Ālūsī defends plowing: the conjunction need not carry every restriction on the first action over to the second; plowing may be illustrative, or the word may mean digging, since plowing does not fit grapes, olives, and palms. Al-Ālūsī objects that intervening human plowing disrupts the sequence of divine gifts."}, {"id": "80:27/q01/p3", "position": "The earlier splitting is the emergence of springs, with rivers flowing from the rain before crops grow.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this interpretation, then objects that 'then' places splitting after the poured water. He also argues that crops following both rain and spring water fits poorly with 78:14–15, where rain alone brings forth grain."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q02", "question": "Why are growing and the preceding acts attributed to God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q02/p1", "position": "The attribution expresses God's governance of the causes that produce water and plants.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the attribution of pouring, splitting, and growing a rational metaphor, though usage makes pouring and planting almost literal; God orders effective causes, sets their laws, and inspires people to use them. Al-Ālūsī says the paired verbs and verbal nouns convey an extraordinary divine provision beyond familiar custom and maintain the focus on God's act."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q03", "question": "What does 'in it' refer to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q03/p1", "position": "It refers to the earth in which God grows the grain.", "reasons": "Bursevi specifies the earth split by the emerging plants; Ṭabāṭabāʾī expressly identifies the pronoun as Earth. Al-Wāḥidī says God grows grain in the earth."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q04", "question": "What does 'grain' include here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q04/p1", "position": "It is grain generally: harvested crops and cereals used as food, especially staple grains.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Ibn Kathīr include all kinds. Al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī give wheat and barley; al-Ālūsī adds maize, Abū Ḥayyān adds corn and lentils, and al-Qurṭubī adds sult. Al-Zajjāj and al-Zamakhsharī stress what is harvested; al-Qurṭubī and al-Ālūsī add storage. Al-Wāḥidī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Nasafī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr stress human nourishment or staples. Al-Biqāʿī includes seeds eaten by both people and animals and says connected growth enables nourishment and development. Bursevī says the collective term may denote a little or a lot. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates the wording to the grain with seven ears in 2:261."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q05", "question": "Why is grain named first among the foods?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q05/p1", "position": "Grain is the chief or foundational nourishment, with the other produce supplementing it.", "reasons": "Bursevi calls it the basic foundation of food; Iṣlāḥī calls it the chief nourishment and the remaining produce supplements."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q06", "question": "What inward growth does this verse suggest?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q06/p1", "position": "God waters hearts with gnosis, bringing forth the flowers of unity and the lights of spiritual stripping.", "reasons": "This is al-Qushayrī's inward reading of the water and growth."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q07", "question": "What is qadab in the surrounding food list, and who eats it?", "turns_on": "Whether the cut growth is counted as human food or livestock feed.", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q07/p1", "position": "It is greens cut after growing, eaten by people.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports a view that calls it greens because they are cut, and a view that people eat it and that it fattens women."}, {"id": "80:27/q07/p2", "position": "It is cut fodder or herbage for livestock.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī derives the name from cutting after it appears. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports a division assigning both qadab and abb to livestock."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q08", "question": "How are the seven provisions apportioned between people and livestock?", "turns_on": "Whether qadab is human food or livestock feed, and whether livestock itself counts as the seventh human provision.", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q08/p1", "position": "Seven listed foods, including qadab, serve people; abb serves animals.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this division and notes that qadab fattens women; another reported view says qadab is cut greens eaten by people. Al-Qurṭubī identifies the seven provisions as crops through fruit and reserves abb for animals; he illustrates the seven stages of creation with 22:5."}, {"id": "80:27/q08/p2", "position": "Qadab and abb feed livestock; six other foods feed people, and livestock itself is their seventh major provision.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this alternative count."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q09", "question": "What sevenfold saying is reported from the Prophet alongside this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q09/p1", "position": "People were created from seven, provided for from seven, and directed to prostrate on seven parts.", "reasons": "Muqātil reports creation, provision, and being brought forth 'upon seven'; al-Qurṭubī reports seven creation stages, seven provisions, and prostration on seven parts. Their wording of the final seven varies. Al-Qurṭubī illustrates the creation stages with 22:5 and identifies the seven provisions as crops through fruit, with abb for animals."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q10", "question": "What cautionary reports accompany interpretation of the food list?", "turns_on": "The reports concern different speakers and incidents of restraint in interpretation.", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q10/p1", "position": "ʿUmar declined to identify abb, treating speculation beyond the clear wording as needless strain.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports through Anas that ʿUmar recognized the other foods, urged following what is clear and leaving the unknown to God, and cites al-Ḥākim's authentication. Ibn Kathīr explains that Abū Bakr and ʿUmar knew abb was a plant from the earth, as 80:28 and 80:31 show, but sought its precise nature."}, {"id": "80:27/q10/p2", "position": "Ibn ʿAbbās refused to interpret a verse that others might have answered.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports the incident and grades its chain authentic."}, {"id": "80:27/q10/p3", "position": "Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allāh rebuked Ṭulq ibn Ḥabīb for asking about a Quranic verse.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports that Jundub adjured Ṭulq, if Muslim, to leave or stop sitting with him."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q11", "question": "How is the vegetation across verses 27–30 described?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q11/p1", "position": "The growth is entwined or closely interwoven.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās gives this gloss for the description across verses 27–30."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q12", "question": "How does the opening reading 'anā' frame the food account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q12/p1", "position": "It opens a detailed account of God's provision that remains necessarily incomplete.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says ordinary explanation cannot encompass the entire food system and its cosmic relations."}]}

{"id": "80:27/q14", "question": "What does the growth and food passage teach or invite?", "turns_on": "The notes draw different lessons from the same visible provision: resurrection, gratitude and obedience, or reflection on creation and revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q14/p1", "position": "Crop growth demonstrates resurrection and God's power to bring life after decay.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī compares growth after decay with emergence from graves and also recalls divine favor. Al-Biqāʿī says human creation and the food cycle prove resurrection and God's power, making rejection astonishing."}, {"id": "80:27/q14/p2", "position": "The sustaining blessings display God's favor and power, calling for faith, gratitude, worship, and obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says crops recall God's favor. Kur'an Yolu says the passage recalls external blessings sustaining human life after the favors of creation in verses 18–20 and aims to strengthen faith and grateful obedience."}, {"id": "80:27/q14/p3", "position": "Natural provisions invite reflection on divine wisdom and the connection of creation with revelation.", "reasons": "The Study Quran says creation is true and glorifies God; it cites 14:19, 6:73, 59:1, 61:1, 62:1, 64:1, 57:1, 59:24, 3:191, and 45:3, and notes an echo of 79:33."}]}
{"id": "80:27/q15", "question": "How does this food passage connect with the sūra and other verses?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the passage to different contexts: the sūra's resurrection warning, its prior account of human creation, other creation verses, or a grain parable.", "positions": [{"id": "80:27/q15/p1", "position": "It advances the sūra's call to warn receptive people by using creation and food as evidence of resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī relates the warning of those who fear to 79:45 and says resurrection purifies receptive hearts while disbelief despite these signs is astonishing."}, {"id": "80:27/q15/p2", "position": "It moves from the favors of human existence in verses 18–20 to outside blessings that sustain life.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu gives this sequence for the passage starting at 80:24."}, {"id": "80:27/q15/p3", "position": "Its provisions echo 79:33 and the Quran's wider teaching that creation is true, glorifies God, and invites reflection.", "reasons": "The Study Quran cites 14:19, 6:73, 59:1, 61:1, 62:1, 64:1, 57:1, 59:24, 3:191, and 45:3."}, {"id": "80:27/q15/p4", "position": "The word grain recalls the parable of a grain yielding seven ears in 2:261.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr makes this verbal link in both notes."}]}
{"id": "81:10/q01", "question": "What are the ṣuḥuf?", "turns_on": "Whether the pages are deeds records, separate pages announcing recompense, a metaphor for enumeration, or inward pages of the faculties and souls.", "positions": [{"id": "81:10/q01/p1", "position": "The records of people's deeds, written by angels and opened for reckoning.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls each person's record a book delivered by guardian angels. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Māwardī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Biqāʿī specify good and evil deeds; al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī say angels wrote them. Al-Wāḥidī and Ibn al-Jawzī call them the records of Adam's children. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows actual pages unlike familiar pages. Al-Iṣlāḥī cites 81:14; Study Quran cites 18:49, 17:71, 50:17–18, 69:19–29 and 82:11–12 for the books and their contents."}, {"id": "81:10/q01/p2", "position": "Pages of recompense flying to their recipients, distinguished from the scrolls of deeds.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān explicitly distinguishes these pages from deeds scrolls. Marthad ibn Wadāʿah, as reported by al-Kashshāf and al-Ālūsī, says they fly from beneath the Throne; the believer's page describes a high garden and the unbeliever's scorching wind and hot water. Al-Qurṭubī transmits the flight and the believer's receipt. Ibn ʿAṭiyya records the right and left according to recompense; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī give distribution as an alternative."}, {"id": "81:10/q01/p3", "position": "A metaphor for whatever enumerates people's deeds.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr presents this alongside the possibility of actual, unfamiliar pages."}, {"id": "81:10/q01/p4", "position": "The pages of the faculties and souls that contain deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says they are folded at death when the spirit's sun is rolled up and opened at resurrection and return to the body."}]}
{"id": "81:10/q02", "question": "What does nushirat describe happening to the scrolls?", "turns_on": "Whether nashr is the opening of folded records for reckoning or their distribution and flight to recipients.", "positions": [{"id": "81:10/q02/p1", "position": "Records folded at death are spread open on Resurrection Day for their owners to read and for judgment.", "reasons": "Qatāda says the filled or dictated record is folded then opened; Muqātil, Ibn Jurayj, al-Māwardī, al-Qurṭubī and others locate folding at death and opening at resurrection or reckoning. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Baghawī compare the spread pages of 74:52; Ibn ʿĀshūr defines nashr as undoing a scroll's folds to read its writing and compares 74:52 and 17:13. Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī cite 18:49 for each owner's seeing the contents. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says each receives a record in the right or left hand; Muqātil and al-Zajjāj likewise mention guardian angels or the hand corresponding to deeds. Al-Biqāʿī says the blessed receive theirs before them in the right hand, the wretched behind their backs in the left. Küran Yolu adds that all good and evil deeds are recalled and judged, citing 69:19–28, 17:13–14 and 18:49."}, {"id": "81:10/q02/p2", "position": "The pages are distributed or fly to their recipients, right or left according to their recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī report distribution as an alternative. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports pages flying right and left according to recompense; Abū Ḥayyān calls these distinct from deed scrolls. Marthad's report in al-Kashshāf, al-Qurṭubī and al-Ālūsī places their flight from beneath the Throne, with the believer receiving a page of high garden and, in the fuller versions, the unbeliever one of scorching wind and hot water."}]}
{"id": "81:10/q03", "question": "How is nushirat read, and what does each form suggest?", "turns_on": "The transmitted vocalizations, the force of 74:52's munashshara, plural morphology, and whether doubling conveys repetition, plurality or intensity; al-Naḥḥās insists both forms are sound.", "positions": [{"id": "81:10/q03/p1", "position": "With a light shīn, nushirat.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī names most Medinans and some Kufans; al-Thaʿlabī names Medina, Syria and Basra except Abū ʿAmr; al-Māwardī says the other readers. Later lists include Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, al-Aʿraj, al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Qatāda, Yaʿqūb and Sahl, with differences in attribution: al-Jishumī reports Abū ʿAmr, Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim here and an alternative report involving Yaʿqūb; Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim leaves this verb undoubled while doubling sajjirat; al-Jishumī's other report puts Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr in the doubled group. Al-Farrāʾ says ordinary Arabic manshūra and plural usage permit the light form; al-Naḥḥās says grammarians allow it for few or many and rejects making 74:52's munashshara decisive against it. Al-Māwardī takes the light form as unfolding once."}, {"id": "81:10/q03/p2", "position": "With a doubled shīn, nushshirat.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī names some Meccans and most Kufans; al-Māwardī names Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī; Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Samīn, al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī also name Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr. Al-Jishumī reports Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr doubling this verb while leaving the neighbouring sajjirat and suʿʿirat undoubled, though his reports differ. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī invoke 74:52's munashshara and the plural's capacity for doubled forms; al-Ṭabarī contrasts singular usage. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the doubling emphasis. Al-Māwardī takes it as repeated unfolding; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī say emphasis, many pages or forceful dispersal; Ibn ʿĀshūr says many scrolls; Qiraat-ER gives thorough, repeated or successive spreading as possible Form II senses."}]}
{"id": "81:10/q04", "question": "What does the opened record reveal or demand of its owner?", "turns_on": "The notes give complementary functions of disclosure, proof, repeated review or emotional effect, and moral warning; al-Māwardī ties the alternatives to once versus repeated unfolding.", "positions": [{"id": "81:10/q04/p1", "position": "It makes every deed visible and establishes the basis of reckoning and proof.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says a single unfolding establishes proof and cites 18:49 for the owner seeing the contents; al-Qurṭubī cites the same verse. The Prophet's answer to Umm Salamah describes records containing dust- and mustard-seed weights. Küran Yolu says people see and recall good and evil before judgment, with 69:19–28, 17:13–14 and 18:49; Study Quran says no deed is hidden and cites 18:49 and other record passages. Al-Iṣlāḥī connects the display of every deed to 81:14. Al-Biqāʿī says the record will save or ruin its owner."}, {"id": "81:10/q04/p2", "position": "Repeated unfolding intensifies rebuke for sinners and glad tidings for the obedient.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī offers this as one explanation of the doubled reading's repeated unfolding."}, {"id": "81:10/q04/p3", "position": "Repeated unfolding lets the person and angel witnesses review the record repeatedly.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī offers this as a second explanation of repeated unfolding."}, {"id": "81:10/q04/p4", "position": "The impending record calls people to guard what they write in it.", "reasons": "Qatāda, reported by al-Kashshāf and Ibn Kathīr, tells each person to watch what is written. Al-Biqāʿī says to put only good words, deeds and beliefs into the record because it will save or ruin its owner. ʿUmar says on reciting the verse that the matter is carried to God, son of

{"id": "81:10/q05", "question": "What did the Prophet tell Umm Salamah about the Resurrection and the records?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "81:10/q05/p1", "position": "People rise barefoot and naked, but are too occupied by the spread records, containing even minute deeds, to attend to women.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī transmits the resurrection statement and Umm Salamah's question separately; al-Kashshāf gives the combined exchange. The records include dust- and mustard-seed weights."}]}
{"id": "81:10/q06", "question": "How does the opening of the records fit the sequence and message of the sūra?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the sign either to the immediately preceding questioning or to the larger arc from cosmic signs and the previous sūra to final judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "81:10/q06/p1", "position": "It begins the signs of each person's coming bliss or punishment after the preceding universal questioning.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī explicitly places the opening of records after the universal questioning. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the listed events descriptions of the Day of Resurrection. Al-Iṣlāḥī places exposed records among the post-resurrection sorting, justice for the oppressed, reddening sky, Hell, Paradise and each person's seeing what was prepared."}, {"id": "81:10/q06/p2", "position": "The sequence announces the Hour and culminates in each soul knowing its deeds at final judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī relates the cosmic signs here to the flight from relatives in 80:33–34 and says the sūra answers when the Hour will come. He also relates the warning to ingratitude in 80:17 and denial of the Qur'an, described as a reminder on honored, pure pages borne by trusted angels. Elmalılı reports Abū ʿĀliya's division into six worldly signs from sun through seas and six afterlife signs from paired souls through approaching Paradise; Elmalılı says their culmination is the great resurrection."}]}
{"id": "81:10/q07", "question": "Why does each sign have its own conditional opening?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "81:10/q07/p1", "position": "Each repeated condition draws attention to a distinct awesome event, while one answer belongs to the conditions together.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says a single opening condition could have sufficed, but repetition gives each event its own force and the answer is attached collectively."}]}
{"id": "81:10/q08", "question": "Can the signs also describe a person's lesser resurrection at death?", "turns_on": "Whether applying the sequence to death is a compatible secondary analogy or an illicit replacement of its apparent account of the great resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "81:10/q08/p1", "position": "They can yield a secondary analogy to death while their primary subject remains the great resurrection.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reports interpreters applying the events to the lesser resurrection and Nīsābūrī presenting the apparent sense first. He says the details of resurrection remain unknown, so possible metaphors help imagine the great event through the certain lesser one and strengthen faith; such reflections do not deny the final resurrection and culminate in it. He cites 3:7 and 59:2. Al-Qāshānī specifically reads the books as faculties' and souls' pages, folded at death when the spirit's sun is rolled up and opened when the body is restored."}, {"id": "81:10/q08/p2", "position": "The signs allegorize the human being and circumstances of death, with the sun as self and stars as senses.", "reasons": "Elmalılı attributes this view to a group cited by Ibn ʿAṭiyya; the transmitted examples concern the sequence of signs."}, {"id": "81:10/q08/p3", "position": "Such symbolic treatment is a Bāṭinī or extreme Sufi departure from clear Arabic exegesis.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reports Abū Ḥayyān's charge that the group's symbolic reading is a cover for covert rejection of Islam, and his broader denial of inner symbols. Elmalılı rejects the severity of the polemic in separate notes."}]}
{"id": "81:10/q09", "question": "What bounds should govern inward or symbolic interpretation of this passage?", "turns_on": "Whether clear Arabic excludes all inner indications, permits those consistent with the apparent text, or is displaced by interpretations that annul decisive meanings and rulings.", "positions": [{"id": "81:10/q09/p1", "position": "Keep the clear Arabic and apparent sense primary, while accepting compatible inward indications and insights.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says the text is clear Arabic, normally read in its apparent sense unless context prevents it; it also has difficult and ambiguous passages and figurative, implicit and rhetorical forms. He affirms outward and inward meaning, tafsīr and taʾwīl, citing reports of outward, inward, limit and ascent. Their agreement follows from 4:82; he compares their meeting to the bounded seas of 55:19–20 and the inexhaustibility of insights to 18:109. Qur'anic address suits differing capacities, with 6:99, 13:4, 2:230, 10:24, 6:126, 6:98, 2:118, 10:6 and 3:190; 3:18 supports learned justice. Compatible Sufi commentaries can retain outward rulings, and attention to intellectual and moral levels serves illumination."}, {"id": "81:10/q09/p2", "position": "Clear Arabic admits no inner symbols, riddles or philosophical and naturalist allusions in exegesis.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, as quoted by Elmalılı, cites 26:195 for clear Arabic; he censures al-Rāzī's use of philosophers, astrologers and astronomers and Sufi statements called 'truths' in Taḥrīr and Taḥbīr. He calls the symbolic reading Bāṭinī or extreme Sufi. Elmalılı calls that polemic excessive."}, {"id": "81:10/q09/p3", "position": "Distortive esotericism abandons decisive passages and cancels their apparent meanings and rulings.", "reasons": "Elmalılı rejects the method associated with Ḥasan Ṣabbāḥ and extreme Imāmite books, distinguishing al-Qāshānī and ʿArāʾis from it. He cites 3:7 against pursuing ambiguous passages for discord. His claim that extreme literalism and esotericism both harm interpretation also invokes 3:18."}]}
{"id": "81:10/q10", "question": "What distinctions does al-Jurjānī make among compound similes?", "turns_on": "The first likeness depends on a full arrangement of components; the second on a familiar relation between paired things.", "positions": [{"id": "81:10/q10/p1", "position": "One kind requires all components in a particular arrangement for the likeness to hold.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says detailed similes have many common patterns and their finest distinctions resist complete enumeration. His example likens narcissus to pearl bowls containing agate; removing a component or changing its relation destroys the intended likeness. These notes state a general rhetorical principle and do not explicitly apply it to this verse."}, {"id": "81:10/q10/p2", "position": "Another kind compares the configuration of paired things rather than either thing alone.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī compares dawn beneath night to a gray horse beneath its covering. The paired configuration is observed and familiar, not merely imagined. These notes do not explicitly identify such a simile in this verse."}]}

{"id": "87:5/q12", "question": "What ancient setting and timescale does the coal account describe?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:5/q12/p1", "position": "A very long sequence of luxuriant ancient growth, submergence, decay and burial produced coal.", "reasons": "The cited Keşfü’l-Esrâr account imagines an initially flat water-covered earth, large early algae and sulfur-family plants, pre-animal coal flora and mountains burying plants.
